p: The book opens like a Greek lecture or speech: a thesis to prove, then proofs.
b: The Greek word is logos, "speech" or "argument", and the speaker addresses his hearers as "you" throughout. 4 Maccabees is not a chronicle like 1 Maccabees or an abridged history like 2 Maccabees but a philosophical speech that proves one claim, first by reasoning and examples from the law (1:13-3:18), then by the martyrs (3:19 to the end). Harry Orlinsky called it an elaborate, philosophical and dramatic variation on the theme of 2 Maccabees' martyr stories. Eusebius and Jerome knew the work under the title On the Sovereignty of Reason, which may be its original name.

p: The book's thesis phrase: reason guided by reverence for God. English versions say "devout" or "pious" reason.
b: Ho eusebēs logismos joins the Greek philosophers' word for the reasoning mind (logismos) to eusebēs, "godly", the word for reverence toward God lived out (godliness, eusebeia, is the virtue of 5:24). The phrase returns at 1:7, 6:31 and at the turning points of the speech. Older English renders it "religious reasoning" (Brenton) and modern ones "devout" or "pious reason". The point of the adjective is the book's whole argument: not any reason, but reason trained by God's law (1:17; 2:23), masters the passions. Codex Venetus leaves the adjective out here (see the variant).

p: A rare Greek word for one who answers to no other master. The book uses several words for rule; each keeps one English word.
b: Autodespotos, "its own master", is used again at 1:30. Beside it stand autokratōr, "sovereign" (1:7, 13, 30), despotēs, "master" (6:31), krateō, "rule", and epikrateō, "overcome" (1:3 and often). The Plain English Translation keeps one English word for each, so that the reader can follow the speaker's piling up of titles: reason is master, sovereign, ruler and leader (1:30), while the passions are its subjects. The language is that of kings and tyrants, and it prepares for the book's contrast between reason's rule and the tyrant Antiochus, whose rule fails (5:38).

p: Pathē: the emotions and drives, the philosophers' word. Pleasure and pain are their two roots (1:20).
b: Ta pathē are things a person "undergoes" (paschō, "suffer, undergo"): emotions, appetites and drives. The Stoics counted four main kinds, pleasure and distress, appetite and fear, defined by whether a good or a bad seems present or still to come. 4 Maccabees uses the same family (1:20-23) but does not agree with the Stoic claim that a wise person feels no passions at all: reason rules them, it does not root them out (1:6; 3:5). Paul uses the same word: "Those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh, with its passions and its desires" (Galatians 5:24).

p: Phronēsis, practical wisdom, is the first of the four virtues; 1:19 calls it the ruler of the others.
b: Phronēsis is the wisdom that sees what to do; older English said "prudence" (Brenton). The speaker calls it the greatest virtue here and the one that rules the rest at 1:19, so the speech in praise of reason is also a speech in praise of good sense. The same word stands among the virtues in the Wisdom of Solomon, where the site's Plain English Translation has "understanding": "She teaches self-control and understanding, / righteousness and courage" (Wisdom of Solomon 8:7). 4 Maccabees keeps its own list of four (see 1:18).

p: Sōphrosynē, "self-restraint", is one of the four virtues; 5:34's enkrateia, "self-control", is kept apart.
b: Sōphrosynē was the Greek virtue of a sound, moderate mind, defined at 1:31 as "mastery over the cravings"; older English said "temperance". The Plain English Translation calls it "self-restraint" and calls its owner "self-restrained" (the "self-restrained mind", 1:35; 2:16). A different word, enkrateia, "self-control", appears in Eleazar's speech (5:34), and it is the word of Galatians 5:23 ("gentleness, self-control"). Keeping the two apart shows that the book's main virtue word is the philosophers' sōphrosynē.

p: Epithymia: the word of the tenth commandment in Greek, rendered "crave" so that 2:5 matches Exodus and Romans.
b: Epithymia is desire that reaches for what it does not have; at 1:22 it is the passion that comes before pleasure. The Plain English Translation renders it "craving" everywhere in the book, because the same word stands in the Greek of the tenth commandment, which 2:5 quotes, and in Paul's "I would not have known what craving was if the law had not said, 'You must not crave'" (Romans 7:7). The site's Exodus 20:17 also says "You must not crave your neighbor's wife".

p: Dikaiosynē here is the civic virtue of giving each their due, so "justice" rather than the Bible's usual "righteousness".
b: The site renders dikaiosynē "righteousness" in most books and notes where "justice" is meant. In 4 Maccabees it is one of the four Greek virtues, the habit of dealing fairly with others (5:24 explains it: "so that we deal fairly with everyone in all our ways"), so "justice" fits. The passion that blocks it is "malice" (kakoētheia, "bad character"), the frame of mind of 1:25 that takes many shapes.

p: If reason rules the passions, why can it not stop forgetting? The speaker calls the objection laughable.
b: The objection plays on the word "passions": forgetting and ignorance are things the mind "undergoes" too. The answer (1:6) is that reason rules the passions that fight the virtues, not its own weaknesses. The speaker raises the same objection again at 2:24-3:1, perhaps because his speech was built from set pieces, or to mark the start of a new section. Either way the answer is the same and sharpened there: reason rules the passions of the body, and it can help against a passion without cutting it out (3:2-5).

a: not so as to destroy them
p: The book's answer to the Stoics: reason does not kill the passions but refuses to give in to them.
b: The Stoics argued that a virtuous person feels no passions and that the happy life is free of them (apathēs). 4 Maccabees says plainly that reason does not "destroy" the passions (here) and is "not the one who pulls up the passions by the roots" but the one "who wrestles against them" (3:5). Its Eleazar and its mother feel pain and love to the full and still choose the law. Reason here is a ruler that keeps the passions in their place, not a surgeon that cuts them out, and the book ties that rule to its claim that the law trains reason.

a: Eleazar, and seven brothers and their mother
p: The proof comes from the martyrs whose story 2 Maccabees tells: the old Eleazar and a mother with seven sons.
b: 2 Maccabees tells of Eleazar, "one of the foremost scribes", who chose death over eating pork (2 Maccabees 6:18-31), and of seven brothers and their mother who died one after another before the king (2 Maccabees 7). 4 Maccabees retells both at great length (5:1-17:6), adds speeches and the mother's inner struggle, and makes them the proof of its thesis. Hebrews recalls such martyrs: "Others were tortured on the rack and would not take the release they were offered" (Hebrews 11:35). The Orthodox churches keep their feast on 1 August as the Holy Maccabees.

p: A hint that the speech was given on a day that remembered the martyrs. Codex Venetus reads "at that time".
b: Kata touton ton kairon, "at this season" or "at this time", has been read as a sign that the speech was delivered on a fixed occasion. The Encyclopaedia Judaica calls the book a philosophical sermon plainly meant for delivery, since otherwise the mention of its "occasion" would mean nothing. It doubts that it was a synagogue sermon, because such sermons seem always to have been built on a verse of Scripture. Ewald and Freudenthal thought of a homily at Hanukkah; the Encyclopaedia Judaica answers that no link between that festival and the martyrs is known, and thinks an assembly at the martyrs' supposed tomb, perhaps at Antioch, on a day of remembrance more likely. Codex Venetus has "at that time" (see the variant), which would remove the hint.

p: Antiochus IV is "the tyrant" all through the book, the Greek picture of the lawless ruler.
b: Ho tyrannos was the Greek name for a ruler who governs by force and not by law. The noun comes 44 times in Swete's Greek of 4 Maccabees, and Antiochus is the tyrant of the story; and the speaker's contrast is pointed: reason is the true sovereign (1:7), and the tyrant, for all his wheels and fires, cannot rule the reasoning of a godly man (5:38). The site keeps "tyrant" where the story shows cruelty (as in 2 Maccabees 7:27) and uses "absolute ruler" in the Wisdom of Solomon, where the word is neutral.

a: so that through them the homeland was cleansed
p: The first hint of the book's claim that the martyrs' deaths did something for the nation. See 6:28-29 and 17:20-22.
b: The verb is katharizō, "cleanse, purify". Two claims are joined: the martyrs' endurance broke the tyranny, and through them the land was cleansed. The first is political (2 Maccabees 8:5 has God's anger turn to mercy as soon as Judas takes up arms), the second is the language of worship, used for the purifying of the temple and the people. Eleazar's prayer makes it explicit, "Make my blood their cleansing" (6:29), and near the end of the book the speaker uses the same verb again: the tyrant was punished and the homeland cleansed (17:21). See the chapter page for chapter 6.

a: giving glory to the all-wise God
p: The philosophical speech is also an act of worship: it begins and ends in praise of God.
b: Ho pansophos theos, "the all-wise God". The speaker gives the same title to Jacob ("our all-wise father", 2:19), so wisdom is first God's and then that of those who live by his law (1:17). The book closes with a doxology too (18:24). Paul ends Romans the same way: "to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory for all the ages" (Romans 16:27).

p: A definition in the philosophers' style: reason is the mind, joined to right living, choosing wisdom's word.
b: The speech now defines its terms, as Greek teachers did (1:14). Logismos is not reason in the abstract but the thinking mind (nous) at work, and the definition ties it to a way of life. The site's other books render logismos "reasoning" or "thoughts" (the Wisdom of Solomon), but here it is the faculty that rules, so the Plain English Translation says "reason". The manuscripts differ on the definition itself: Codex Sinaiticus and Venetus have "right reason" for "right life" (see the variant).

a: the knowledge of things divine and human, and of their causes
p: Cicero gives the same definition of wisdom and says the old philosophers made it.
b: Cicero wrote: "Wisdom, as the old philosophers defined it, is the knowledge of things divine and human and of the causes that hold them together" (On Duties 2.5, in Latin). 4 Maccabees uses the same school definition in Greek. The real link is not borrowing from Cicero but a shared stock of Greek teaching. What the speaker does with it is new: the next verse says that this wisdom is "the training the law gives" (1:17). Proverbs makes a different start: "The fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins" (Proverbs 1:7).

a: This is the training the law gives
t: Compared with the Bible: the law as wisdom
p: The philosophers' wisdom is the law of Moses. The Bible says something close; Paul says something different.
b: Paideia is education, upbringing and discipline. The site's Sirach says "discipline" for it by default, but the Plain English Translation of 4 Maccabees says "training" wherever the sense is schooling in the law, as here: the book pictures the law as a school that trains the mind, the way a Greek teacher trained his pupils, not as correction or punishment. The verb paideuō is "schools" at 5:24, and paideutēs "teacher" at 5:34. The speaker claims that the Torah is the school of true wisdom. Agrees with Deuteronomy, where keeping the laws "will show your wisdom and your understanding to the peoples" (compare Deuteronomy 4:6), and with Psalm 19:7 and Psalm 119:98. Goes beyond them in casting the law as a philosophy that trains the four Greek virtues. Paul agrees that the law is holy (Romans 7:12) but denies that it gives power over sin: "What the law brings is knowledge of sin" (Romans 3:20). See the note on 2:23.
orig: ἡ τοῦ νόμου παιδεία (hē tou nomou paideia)
r: Deuteronomy 4:6; Psalm 19:7; Psalm 119:98; Romans 7:12; Romans 3:20; Sirach 24:23

a: good sense, justice, courage and self-restraint
p: The four virtues of Greek philosophy, later called the "cardinal" virtues by Christian teachers.
b: Plato's Republic names the four when Socrates describes the good city: "Clearly, then, it will be wise, brave, sober, and just" (Republic 4.427e). The Wisdom of Solomon lists the same four as the fruits of Wisdom (Wisdom of Solomon 8:7). The Catholic Catechism calls them "cardinal" because "all the others are grouped around them" and quotes the Wisdom of Solomon for them (Catechism 1805). 4 Maccabees makes them "kinds of wisdom", which here means the law (1:17), and it shows each in the martyrs: Eleazar's self-restraint at the table, his courage under the whip, his justice toward the law.

p: The speaker sorts the passions under pleasure and pain, as the Stoics did, with craving and fear before them.
b: The Stoics counted four main kinds of passion: pleasure (a present good), distress (a present bad), appetite (a good still to come) and fear (a bad still to come). 1:22-23 has the same four in its own order: craving comes before pleasure and fear before pain, with joy and grief after them. Anger (1:24) and malice (1:25) are added. The sorting is the common stock of Greek moral teaching, and the speaker uses it to show that everything a person feels falls under reason's rule.

p: In this list joy is the feeling that follows pleasure, not the joy of the Spirit in Paul.
b: Chara, "joy", is the word for the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), but here it is simply the glad feeling after a pleasure, as grief (lypē) is the feeling after a pain. The Stoics kept a separate set of "good feelings" for the wise, responses to real goods; this speaker does not draw that line. Readers should not import Paul's meaning into the list.

p: Boasting, love of money, love of glory, love of quarreling and envy: the forms malice takes in the soul.
b: The list uses compound words built on phil-, "love of": philargyria (love of money, the word of 1 Timothy 6:10, "A root of every kind of evil is the love of money"), philodoxia (love of glory) and philoneikia (love of quarreling; compare Luke 22:24). Baskania, "envy", is literally the evil eye. Codex Venetus has kenodoxia, "empty glory", for love of glory. The list is of a kind common in Greek moral writing, like the lists of vices in Romans 1:29-31 and Galatians 5:19-21.

p: Monophagia: eating by oneself so as not to share, counted with gluttony as a vice of the body.
b: Monophagia is a rare word for eating alone, the greedy habit of keeping one's food from others; the man who "by nature eats alone" comes back at 2:7. In Greek and Jewish life a shared table was a mark of friendship and generosity. Swete prints monophagia; his footnote says Codex Alexandrinus has the slip nomophagia. Codex Sinaiticus puts "eating alone" before "gorging", and Codex Venetus lacks "gorging" (see the variant). The first word in the list, pantophagia, "eating anything at all", fits the theme that follows: the law limits what may be eaten (1:33-34).

a: Reason is the gardener over all of them
p: Reason tends the passions like a farmer: weeding, pruning, tying up and watering. It tames them; it does not kill them.
b: The rare word pangeōrgos means "farmer of all". The image follows from 1:28, where pleasure and pain are plants with many shoots. The gardener does not tear the plants out; he trims and trains them and "tames the wild thickets" (the Greek hylē is woodland or brush). The last verb, metacheōn, is not clear: the lexicon of Liddell and Scott gives "pour from one vessel into another", and in a garden that may mean moving a plant to a new bed or pot. Brenton's English has "transplanting"; the Plain English Translation says "moves it from place to place". The picture fits the book's claim that reason rules the passions without uprooting them (3:5).

p: The three groups of animals the law sorts into clean and unclean, in a different order from Leviticus 11.
b: The list has the same three groups as the food laws of Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14, in a different order. Both of those chapters begin with the animals of the land (Leviticus 11:2-8; Deuteronomy 14:4-8), then the water creatures ("you may eat these: anything in the seas or the streams that has fins and scales", Leviticus 11:9), then the birds (Leviticus 11:13-19; Deuteronomy 14:11-20). The speaker starts with the sea. The speaker's argument is that keeping these laws is proof that reason can master appetite, since the forbidden foods are often desirable. The test of the martyrs will be just this law: pork (5:2; Deuteronomy 14:8).

p: Joseph refused his master's wife (Genesis 39). The speaker makes him the model of reason ruling sexual desire.
b: Genesis tells how Joseph, a young slave in Egypt, refused his master's wife day after day: "So how could I do this great evil and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9). When she grabbed him, "he left his garment in her hand and ran outside" (Genesis 39:12). Genesis gives the reason as loyalty to his master and fear of God. 4 Maccabees retells it as a victory of reason over the strongest passion. Jewish writers of the Greek period often praised Joseph's self-restraint; Philo wrote a life of him.

p: Oistros was a gadfly whose sting drove cattle wild; the Greeks used it for any mad passion, above all lust.
b: The Greek oistros is the gadfly, and then the frenzy its sting causes. 2:4 uses the related oistrēlasia, the "goad" of desire, and 3:17 speaks of the "fevers of their frenzies". The Plain English Translation keeps the picture rather than flattening it to "lust": the passion is something that drives a person from outside, and reason is the one who stands firm against it.

a: You must not crave your neighbor's wife, or anything at all that belongs to your neighbor
p: A shortened quotation of the tenth commandment, in the order of the Greek, with the wife first.
b: The Hebrew of Exodus lists the house first and then the wife ("You must not crave your neighbor's house. You must not crave your neighbor's wife", Exodus 20:17). The Hebrew of Deuteronomy 5:21 puts the wife first, and so does the Greek of both passages as Swete prints Codex Vaticanus; the quotation here follows that Greek word for word in its first and last clauses. It ends with the summary clause, "anything at all that belongs to your neighbor". Paul quotes the same commandment in two words: "You must not crave" (Romans 7:7).

a: Now since the law has told us not to crave
t: Compared with the Bible: the tenth commandment and Romans 7
p: 4 Maccabees reads "do not crave" as proof that reason can master craving. Paul reads it as the law that showed him his sin.
b: The speaker argues: the law would not command what is impossible, so reason can rule craving. Paul, quoting the same commandment, says: "Sin found its opening in the commandment, and it produced in me every kind of craving" (Romans 7:8), and "with my mind I myself serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin" (Romans 7:25). The two readings conflict on what the law can do in a person, though both honor it. Readers have long set the passages side by side; see the "Where Christians differ" card on this chapter.

p: Lending without interest to a fellow Israelite in need, and the release of debts in the seventh year.
b: The law forbids taking interest from a poor fellow Israelite (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35-37) and orders a release of debts every seventh year: "Every lender is to let go of the loan he made to his neighbor" (Deuteronomy 15:2). The Greek "the sevens" (hebdomades) means the sabbatical years. The speaker's point is that the law forces even a lover of money to act against his nature, so it trains reason against greed. Swete prints enstasōn ("when the seventh years come") from Codex Sinaiticus and Venetus; his footnote gives Alexandrinus's slip entassōn.

a: He does not glean the leftovers of his harvests
p: The law leaves the edges of fields and the last grapes for the poor and the foreigner.
b: "Do not pick your vineyard clean, and do not gather the fallen grapes of your vineyard. Leave them for the poor and for the foreigner" (Leviticus 19:10; compare Leviticus 23:22; Deuteronomy 24:19-21). Ruth gleaned in Boaz's field under this law (Ruth 2:2-3). The speaker uses it as a cure for stinginess: a law that a stingy man must obey teaches his reason to rule his passion.

a: it does not betray virtue for their sake
t: When love must yield to the law
p: Deuteronomy 13 names the same circle of nearest family: even they must not be followed into idolatry.
b: The speaker lists the strongest loves, for parents, a wife, children and friends, and says the law rules them all. The list can be set beside Deuteronomy 13:6, which names the same circle: "Your brother, your own mother's son ... your son or your daughter, or the wife you hold close, or the friend who is like your own self", who might say, "Let us go and serve other gods". Children who are rebellious may be punished (Deuteronomy 21:18-21). Jesus too says that love for him must come before family (Matthew 10:37). The thought prepares for the mother of chapters 14-16, whose love for her sons yields to godly reason.

a: So a person does not cut down the enemy's orchard trees
t: Kindness to enemies in the law
p: The law spares an enemy's fruit trees and orders help with an enemy's animals.
b: The speaker gathers three laws. In war, fruit trees are not to be destroyed: "You may eat from them, but do not cut them down" (Deuteronomy 20:19). An enemy's stray animal is to be returned: "If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey straying, you must bring it back to him" (Exodus 23:4). A fallen animal is to be helped up (Exodus 23:5; Deuteronomy 22:4). All of them, he says, make reason master over hatred. Proverbs 25:21 and Jesus' "love your enemies" (Matthew 5:44) carry the same line further.

p: Numbers 16 says Moses "grew very angry" at the rebels, but he left the judgment to the LORD.
b: When Dathan and Abiram refused his summons, "Moses grew very angry and said to the LORD, 'Do not turn toward their offering'" (Numbers 16:15). Moses then let the LORD decide between him and the rebels, and the earth swallowed them (Numbers 16:28-33). The speaker reads this as reason ruling anger: Moses felt it, but did not act on it. The verb is diaitaō, "to settle as an arbitrator", so reason is pictured as the judge over the passion.

p: Jacob's last words on his sons' massacre at Shechem (Genesis 34; 49:5-7).
b: After the rape of their sister Dinah, Simeon and Levi took their swords and "killed every male" of Shechem (Genesis 34:25). On his deathbed Jacob said: "Their anger be cursed, for it was savage" (Genesis 49:7). The speaker draws from it that anger can and should be ruled by reason, since Jacob would not curse what cannot be helped. The Greek of Genesis 49:7 calls their anger "self-willed" (authadēs); Codex Venetus adds that word here too (see the variant). Other Jewish writings of the time praised the brothers' zeal instead (Judith 9:2-4).

a: For when God fashioned the human being
t: Compared with the Bible: the mind and the law
p: God made the passions, put the mind on a throne over them, and gave it the law. Genesis says nothing of the kind in so many words.
b: The speaker tells creation in Greek terms: the passions and habits are planted around the human being by God himself, so they are not evil in themselves ("God looked at everything he had made, and there it was, very good", Genesis 1:31). The mind is enthroned as "holy leader" (hēgemōn, the philosophers' word for the ruling part of the soul) and receives the law. Agrees with Genesis that God made people to rule (Genesis 1:28) and that he gave a command at once (Genesis 2:16-17). Goes beyond Genesis in its picture of the soul, and this passage says nothing of the fall (the serpent appears later, in the mother's words at 18:8). Paul, by contrast, says the law was powerless "because the flesh made it weak" (Romans 8:3).

a: it will be king over a self-restrained, just, good and courageous kingdom
p: The mind that keeps the law reigns as a king; the four virtues become the marks of its kingdom.
b: The Greek has "he will reign a kingdom", a doubled phrase like "rule a rule". The four qualities echo the four virtues of 1:18, with "good" in place of "good sense". The speaker gives the crown to the mind that lives by the law of Moses. The thought returns in the book's picture of the martyrs: an old man on the ground under the whip is the real king, and the tyrant on his throne is the one defeated (6:10; 9:30).

a: But that reasoning is quite laughable
p: Swete's text uses logismos, "reasoning", for the objector's argument too: the objection itself is poor reasoning.
b: In Codex Alexandrinus the verse begins, "But that logismos is quite laughable", the same word the book uses for reason. The objector reasons badly about reason. Codex Venetus and a corrector of Sinaiticus have the plainer logos, "argument" (see the variant). The first hand of Sinaiticus left out everything from "rules" in 2:24 to "reason" in 3:1 (Swete gives the gap as kratei lēthēs ... heautou pathōn ho logismos), and a corrector wrote the words back in.

a: none of you can cut out craving
t: Compared with the Bible: can craving be cut out?
p: The speaker says no one can cut out craving; he can only refuse to be its slave.
b: The four sentences of 3:2-4 repeat "cannot cut out" (ekkoptō, the word for cutting down a tree). The goal is not freedom from desire but freedom from slavery to it. Agrees with Paul that sin's craving still lives in the body and that the believer must not let it rule: "So do not let sin be your king in your mortal body, with you obeying its desires" (Romans 6:12). Differs in where the power comes from: here, reason trained by the law; in Paul, the Spirit (Romans 8:13; Galatians 5:16).

a: It is the one who wrestles against them
p: Antagōnistēs, a rival in a contest. The book's athletic language begins here.
b: Reason is not the ekrizōtēs, "uprooter", but the antagōnistēs, the opponent in a wrestling match or race. The contest language grows through the book: Eleazar is "a noble athlete" (6:10), and the martyrs' deaths are a holy contest with the world watching (17:11-16). Hebrews 12:4 uses the same picture: "Not yet have you held out to the point of blood in your fight against sin."

p: The Greek Bible often calls the Philistines allophyloi, "people of another race".
b: Allophyloi, "those of another tribe", is the usual Septuagint word for the Philistines, so the Greek-speaking reader would know at once who David's enemies were. 2 Samuel 23:13-14 names a company of Philistines camped in the Valley of Rephaim and a Philistine post at Bethlehem.

p: In 2 Samuel the water is brought by three of David's warriors; here by two young soldiers, after a battle.
b: 2 Samuel 23:13-17 and 1 Chronicles 11:15-19 tell the story briefly: David longed for water "from the well of Bethlehem, the one at the gate"; "the three warriors forced their way through the Philistine camp" and brought it; David would not drink it and "poured it out to the LORD". 4 Maccabees changes the details: a day of battle, a royal tent, grumbling shield-bearers, two young men, a spring in the enemy camp. It also changes the meaning: in Samuel David honors the men's courage, here he masters his own craving.

a: since it was counted as worth the same as blood
p: David's words in Samuel: "The blood of the men who went with their lives at stake?"
b: In 2 Samuel 23:17 David says, "LORD, I could never do this! The blood of the men who went with their lives at stake?" Chronicles is fuller: "Am I to drink the blood of these men, with their lives at stake?" (1 Chronicles 11:19). Because the law forbids eating blood, and "a body's life is in its blood" (Leviticus 17:11), water won at the risk of lives could not be drunk. The speaker adds that drinking it would have been "a terrible danger to his soul".

a: poured the drink out to God
p: The verb is the one for pouring a libation: David turns his craving into an offering.
b: Speudō (here espeisen) is the word for pouring out a drink offering to a god, the Greek of 2 Samuel 23:16's "he poured it out to the LORD". Paul uses the same verb of himself: "I am being poured out as a drink offering" (compare Philippians 2:17; 2 Timothy 4:6). In 4 Maccabees David's libation is the final proof of the first half: reason can defeat even the fiercest bodily craving.

a: spit out every hold the passions take
p: A vivid verb: reason "spits out" the passions' mastery. Eleazar will refuse the pork in the same spirit.
b: Apoptyō means "spit out", and so "reject with disgust". 2 Maccabees has Eleazar literally spitting out the meat (2 Maccabees 6:20, "spitting it out first"). 4 Maccabees never has him put it in his mouth, but here, before the story begins, it uses the same picture for reason's rejection of everything the passions try to impose. "Throw in wrestling" is katapalaiō, another wrestling word.

p: 2 Maccabees 3:3 just says Seleucus. The king meant is Seleucus IV; the epithet is that of Seleucus I, Nicator.
b: The king who paid for the temple sacrifices in 2 Maccabees 3:3 is "Seleucus, king of Asia", the father of Demetrius and the brother of Antiochus IV, who reigned just before him (2 Maccabees 4:7; Appian, Syrian Wars 45). Historians call him Seleucus IV. "Nicanor" seems to confuse him with the founder of the dynasty, Seleucus I, whose epithet was Nicator, "Conqueror". Codex Venetus reads "Seleucus, son of Nicanor" (see the variant). The Roman historian Appian says that Seleucus was killed "as the result of a conspiracy of a certain Heliodorus, one of the court officers", and 2 Maccabees 3:7 names Heliodorus as the king's chief minister, the man sent to take the temple money.

a: he approved their way of life
p: Politeia: the right to live by their own laws, which Greek kings granted and later took away.
b: Politeia means a city's constitution or a people's way of life. The site renders it "way of life" in 2 Maccabees. Seleucid kings confirmed the Jews' right to live under their ancestral laws; 2 Maccabees 4:11 says Jason "pushed aside the favors the kings had granted the Jews". The verb politeuomai, "live as a citizen", runs through this book: to live "by the law" (2:8, 23; 4:23; 5:16) is to be a citizen of God's commonwealth.

p: The quarrel that 2 Maccabees 3:4-4:6 tells: Simon, a temple official, against the high priest Onias III.
b: 2 Maccabees calls Simon "from the tribe of Benjamin, the appointed overseer of the temple", who quarreled with Onias "over the running of the city market" (2 Maccabees 3:4). It is Onias who goes to the king (2 Maccabees 4:5); here Simon flees. Onias III was the high priest whose godliness 2 Maccabees 3:1 praises, later murdered (2 Maccabees 4:33-34). 4 Maccabees says he held office "for life", the old rule before kings began to sell the office.

a: the governor of Syria, Phoenicia and Cilicia
p: 2 Maccabees says Coele-Syria and Phoenicia. This book adds Cilicia, which some scholars use to date it.
b: In 2 Maccabees 3:5 Apollonius is "governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia". The title here adds Cilicia, in what is now southeastern Turkey. James Rochford's summary of David deSilva's Introducing the Apocrypha gives the argument: Syria, Phoenicia and Cilicia were joined into one governmental unit at some point between AD 19 and 72, and deSilva dates the book to the first half of the first century AD. If the title is a clue, the speaker gave Apollonius the office as it stood in his own day. Other dates have been proposed: Elias Bickerman about AD 20-54, Moses Hadas about AD 40, André Dupont-Sommer the reign of Hadrian (AD 118-135), and Jan Willem van Henten the last decades of the first century as plausible too. So proposed dates run from about AD 20 to the early second century.

p: Ancient temples served as banks. 2 Maccabees 3:10-12 names widows and orphans among the depositors.
b: Temples were safe places to keep money, and people left savings there in trust. In 2 Maccabees the high priest explains that the money includes "deposits belonging to widows and orphans" and some belonging to Hyrcanus son of Tobias (2 Maccabees 3:10-11). Simon's claim is that the money is private, not sacred, and so the king may take it. 4:7 gives the people's answer: those who "entrusted their deposits to the temple treasury" would be robbed.

a: He was given authority over the matter
p: In 2 Maccabees the king sends his minister Heliodorus. Here Apollonius goes himself.
b: 2 Maccabees 3:7 has the king send "Heliodorus, his chief minister" to remove the money, and Heliodorus is the one struck down. 4 Maccabees drops Heliodorus and gives his part to Apollonius. The speaker shortens and simplifies the history (4:1-26 covers 2 Maccabees 3-6 in a few verses), since his interest is only to bring the persecution on stage. The Encyclopaedia Judaica says that the details not taken from 2 Maccabees came from the author's own imagination.

p: 2 Maccabees 3:25-26 has a horse with a fearsome rider and two young men. Here they are angels, armed and flashing.
b: In 2 Maccabees "there appeared to them a horse with a fearsome rider" that kicked Heliodorus, and "two other young men" flogged him (2 Maccabees 3:25-26). 4 Maccabees makes them openly angels, with flashing weapons. The Bible has other heavenly armies: the horses and chariots of fire around Elisha (2 Kings 6:17) and the armies of heaven on white horses (Revelation 19:14). Apollonius asks the Hebrews to make peace for him with "the army of heaven" (4:11).

a: the court of the temple that is open to all peoples
p: Pamphylos, "of all tribes": the outer court, where non-Jews could come.
b: The rare word pamphylos means "belonging to all tribes or peoples". The outer court of the temple, later called the Court of the Gentiles, was open to everyone, and Paul was mobbed when people thought "he has brought Greeks into the temple" (Acts 21:28). So Apollonius falls just where a foreigner was allowed to stand. Brenton translates "the court which is open to all nations".
orig: ὁ πάμφυλος τοῦ ἱεροῦ περίβολος (ho pamphylos tou hierou peribolos)

p: As in 2 Maccabees 3:32-33, the high priest intercedes for the man who came to rob the temple.
b: 2 Maccabees 3:32 says, "The high priest grew uneasy that the king might suspect the Jews of some crime against Heliodorus. So he brought a sacrifice for the man's rescue." 4 Maccabees has the same fear but only a prayer, not a sacrifice. The high priest's prayer for a Gentile enemy recalls Abraham praying for Abimelech (Genesis 20:17) and Job praying for his friends (Job 42:10).

p: Antiochus IV was the brother of Seleucus IV, not his son. 2 Maccabees 4:7 does not say how they were related.
b: Antiochus IV was the brother of Seleucus IV, not his son: Appian says Seleucus "gave his son Demetrius as a hostage in place of his brother Antiochus" (Syrian Wars 45). 2 Maccabees 4:7 says only, "Seleucus departed this life, and Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes, received the kingdom". The slip is one of the historical errors that led scholars to doubt that Josephus wrote this book, as Eusebius and Jerome believed. "Epiphanes" means "(god) made manifest".

p: 2 Maccabees 4:8-9 has 360 talents plus 80, and 150 more for the gymnasium. 4 Maccabees has ten times as much.
b: In 2 Maccabees Jason promises "three hundred sixty talents of silver, plus eighty talents out of some other income", and a hundred fifty more for the gymnasium (2 Maccabees 4:8-9). 4 Maccabees has 3,660 a year, perhaps a copyist's or the writer's inflation of 360. The first hand of Codex Sinaiticus had "one thousand six hundred sixty" (see the variant). A talent was a very large sum of silver.

p: The Greek school and sports ground, where young men trained naked. 2 Maccabees places it at the foot of the citadel.
b: The gymnasium was the center of Greek education. 1 Maccabees says, "They built a gymnasium in Jerusalem, following the customs of the nations" (1 Maccabees 1:14), and 2 Maccabees places it "at the very foot of the citadel" (2 Maccabees 4:12). Here it is "on top of" the citadel, a sharper charge. Priests neglected the altar to watch the games (2 Maccabees 4:14), which may be what "put an end to the care of the temple" refers to.

p: Dikē, Justice, is spoken of as a person who is angered and makes war. The book uses the figure often.
b: In Greek thought Dikē was Justice personified, even a goddess. 4 Maccabees uses "divine Justice" as a way to speak of God's judgment without naming God, and she returns at 8:14, 22; 9:9 and 18:22, where she pursues the tyrant. The Plain English Translation capitalizes the word where it acts as a person. At 4:13 the same phrase only names what might have struck Apollonius down, so it is lowercase "divine justice"; at 4:21 Justice is the one who is outraged and makes war. Acts 28:4 has the islanders of Malta say of Paul, "Justice won't let him go on living".

a: He was fighting Ptolemy in Egypt
t: The rumor and the sack of Jerusalem
p: 2 Maccabees 5:5-11 tells of the false report of Antiochus's death and his savage return.
b: Antiochus IV invaded Egypt, then ruled by Ptolemy VI. "A lying report went around that Antiochus had departed this life" (2 Maccabees 5:5), and Jason attacked the city. The king took it as a revolt: "he pulled out of Egypt, savage as a wild beast in spirit, and took the city at spear point" (2 Maccabees 5:11). 4 Maccabees skips Jason's attack and says only that the people rejoiced at the rumor. Daniel 11:28-31 is often read as referring to these events.

p: 1 and 2 Maccabees tell the same horror: mothers killed with the babies they had circumcised.
b: "Following the decree, they put to death the women who had had their children circumcised. They hung the babies from their mothers' necks" (1 Maccabees 1:60-61). 2 Maccabees has two women led around the city and flung from the wall with their babies (2 Maccabees 6:10). The speaker adds that the women knew beforehand what they would suffer, which makes them early witnesses of his thesis, and forerunners of the mother of the seven.

p: Ioudaismos, the word 2 Maccabees first uses for the Jewish way of life, as the opposite of the Greek way.
b: Ioudaismos appears first in 2 Maccabees (2 Maccabees 2:21; 8:1; 14:38), as the opposite of "the Greek way" (2 Maccabees 4:13). Paul uses it of his past: "I was going further in Judaism" (Galatians 1:14). Here the king forces people to "swear off" (exomnymi) Judaism by tasting defiling food: the food law has become the test of loyalty. Antiochus himself enforces it on Eleazar (4:26-5:3), a change from the Eleazar scene of 2 Maccabees, where the men in charge of the sacrificial meal press him (2 Maccabees 6:18-21); in the scene of the seven brothers there the king is present (2 Maccabees 7:3).

p: The book's test case. The law forbids the pig because it splits the hoof but does not chew the cud.
b: The Greek is "meats of swine" (krea hyeia); the Plain English Translation says "pork" every time in this book. "The pig has a split hoof but does not chew the cud. It is unclean for you. Do not eat their meat" (Deuteronomy 14:8). 2 Maccabees has "pig's meat" for Eleazar (2 Maccabees 6:18) and "pork" for the brothers (2 Maccabees 7:1). "Food sacrificed to idols" adds the second offense, the same one the Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to avoid (Acts 15:29).
r: Deuteronomy 14:8; Leviticus 11:7; 2 Maccabees 6:18; 2 Maccabees 7:1; Acts 15:29; 1 Corinthians 8:1

p: Trochizō: to be tied to a wheel and broken. 4 Maccabees is our earliest full account of the torture.
b: The verb trochizō means to torture on the wheel (trochos, 5:32). In the brothers' story the wheel is described at length (9:12-20; 11:10, 17). 2 Maccabees speaks of whips, cords, a torture frame and pans (2 Maccabees 6:19; 7:1-5); but not of a wheel.

a: He was a priest by birth
p: 2 Maccabees calls Eleazar "one of the foremost scribes". Here he is a priest, a lawyer and a philosopher.
b: 2 Maccabees 6:18 has "Eleazar, one of the foremost scribes". 4 Maccabees makes him a priest "by birth" (to genos), an expert in the law (nomikos, the word for the lawyers of the Gospels, Luke 10:25), and later a man known for his philosophy (5:35; 7:7). Why the book makes him a priest is not said; the box on the chapter page gives Claude's theory, that it fits his prayer at 6:28-29. Codex Venetus adds "for his philosophy" to why the court knew him (see the variant). Orthodox tradition keeps him as "the Teacher of the Holy Seven Maccabee Martyrs" (Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, 1 August).

a: you do not seem to me to be a philosopher
p: Antiochus argues like a Greek teacher: a real philosopher would follow nature, not Jewish custom.
b: The tyrant's speech (5:6-13) is a small philosophical debate. Its points: nature gives pork as a gift (5:7-9); a wise man enjoys pleasures that bring no shame (5:8); Jewish religion (thrēskeia) is a babbling philosophy (5:10-11); and any god would forgive what is done under force (5:13). These are serious arguments for a Greek reader, and the speaker lets Antiochus make them well, so that Eleazar's answer (5:16-38) can show that the law itself is the true philosophy.

p: "Follow nature" was a slogan of Greek philosophy. Eleazar answers that the law fits nature (5:25).
b: The Stoics taught that the good life is life in agreement with nature, and Antiochus turns the slogan against the law: if nature made the pig good to eat, refusing it is against nature. Eleazar does not deny that God made nature; he answers that the Creator of the world gave a law that suits our nature (5:25-26). Paul too appeals to "nature" in moral argument (Romans 1:26; 1 Corinthians 11:14), and many Christians read him as saying the food laws no longer bind believers (Romans 14:14), though Messianic Jewish and other Torah-observant readers take that verse differently.

a: Won't you scatter the nonsense of your reasoning?
p: From here to the start of chapter 12, Codex Venetus has lost its pages. Only Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus remain.
b: Swete's footnote at this verse says that the rest is missing in Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD) up to 12:1, where its pages were cut away. So for most of the martyr story, including Eleazar's prayer (6:28-29), the two witnesses Swete cites are Codex Alexandrinus (A, the text he prints) and Codex Sinaiticus. The tyrant mocks the old man's "reasoning" (logismos), the very word of the thesis: the debate is about whose reason is truly reason.

a: it would forgive you for any lawbreaking you do under force
p: The king's best argument: God would excuse what is done under force. Later Jewish law agreed in part.
b: The argument has weight. The Talmud gives Rabbi Yohanan's ruling that a Jew may break the Torah's commands rather than be killed, "except for those of idol worship, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed"; but in a time of persecution, "even if they issued a decree about a minor mitzva, one must be killed and not transgress", and the same holds for an order to sin in public (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 74a, in the Sefaria translation). Eleazar's answer is of that second kind: he is in public, before many, and his act would teach the young (6:19). He also answers that small and great sins weigh the same (5:20).

a: we must live by a divine law
t: Living as citizens of the law
p: Politeuomai: to live as a citizen. The law is the constitution of Eleazar's people.
b: The verb is politeuesthai, "to live as a citizen" (see the note on 3:20). Eleazar answers the king as one citizen of a commonwealth answers another: his people's constitution is divine, and "no force is stronger than our obedience" (eupeitheia). Paul uses the same verb: "live as citizens worthy of the good news of Christ" (Philippians 1:27), and the related noun: "we belong to a commonwealth in heaven" (Philippians 3:20).

a: Even if our law were not truly divine
p: Eleazar grants, for argument's sake, that the law may not be divine, and says he still could not give it up.
b: This is a debating move: even on the king's own terms, a man of reputation for godliness could not throw it away without disgrace. The argument from reputation is the one 2 Maccabees gives Eleazar ("Many young people would suppose that Eleazar, ninety years old, had changed over to foreign ways", 2 Maccabees 6:24). Then he gives his real ground: "We believe that the law was set in place by God" (5:25).

a: To break the law in small things or in great ones weighs the same
t: Compared with the Bible: small and great sins
p: The same principle stands in James 2:10 and in Jesus' words about the least commandments.
b: Agrees with the New Testament: "Someone might keep the entire law and trip over only one command, but he has become answerable for all of it" (James 2:10), and Jesus warns against loosening "even one of the smallest of these commands" (Matthew 5:19). The point is that every law is the one lawgiver's word, so contempt for a small one is contempt for him (5:21). The Mishnah says much the same: "be careful with a light commandment as with a grave one" (Mishnah Avot 2:1, in Joshua Kulp's translation on Sefaria).

p: Eleazar calls the law "our philosophy" and lists the four virtues it teaches (5:23-24).
b: To a Greek, philosophia was the way of life of a school, not just ideas. Eleazar answers the king's mockery (5:10-11) by claiming that the law is a philosophy and a better one, because it teaches all four virtues and, above them, true godliness (5:23-24). Paul warns the Colossians against being carried off "with philosophy, with empty tricks" that "do not follow Christ" (Colossians 2:8), with a quite different aim.

a: only the God who truly is
p: Eleazar's "the God who is" echoes the Greek of Exodus 3:14, "I am the one who is".
b: The Greek ton onta theon, "the God who is", recalls the Greek of Exodus 3:14, where God says, "I am the one who is" (egō eimi ho ōn). It also suits philosophy, where true being belongs to God alone. Godliness (eusebeia) is here added to the four virtues as the crown of the list: the law teaches people to worship the one true God "with fitting honor" (megaloprepōs, "in a way worthy of his greatness").

p: Eleazar's answer to the king: the God who made nature gave the law to suit it.
b: "The Creator of the world" (ho tou kosmou ktistēs) is the title the mother uses in 2 Maccabees 7:23. Eleazar's argument is that creation and law have one author, so the law cannot be against nature; God "shows us a sympathy" (sympathei, "feels with") in his laws. Hebrews uses the same verb of Christ, the high priest who is not "unable to feel for us in our weaknesses" (Hebrews 4:15). The claim that forbidden foods "work against" the soul (5:26) goes beyond the Torah, which grounds the food laws in holiness ("be holy, for I am holy", Leviticus 11:44) but does not say how each forbidden food would harm the soul.

a: the holy oaths our forefathers swore to keep the law
p: Israel swore at Sinai and at the renewals of the covenant to keep the law.
b: At Sinai the people answered, "Every word the LORD has spoken, we will do" (Exodus 24:3); under Nehemiah they took on themselves "a curse and an oath: to walk by God's law" (Nehemiah 10:29). Eleazar counts himself bound by those oaths. His word for "set aside" (pariēmi) means to let go or neglect, the opposite of keeping faith.

p: Enkrateia, the word of Galatians 5:23. Eleazar speaks to the law, self-control, reason and his priesthood as to friends.
b: Eleazar addresses five things as if they were persons: the law, his teacher; self-control; reason, "lover of wisdom" (philosophos logos); the priesthood; and understanding of the law (5:34-35). Enkrateia, "self-control", is the last of the fruits of the Spirit in Galatians 5:23 ("gentleness, self-control") and is kept apart from the book's usual sōphrosynē, "self-restraint" (see 1:3). Codex Sinaiticus reads "I will not swear you off" for "I will not run from you" (see the variant).

a: The fathers will welcome me pure
t: Compared with the Bible: welcomed by the fathers
p: Eleazar expects the patriarchs to receive him at death. 4 Maccabees speaks of souls with the fathers, not of resurrection.
b: The hope is that the dead join the patriarchs; later the speaker says the martyrs stand beside God's throne (17:18) and that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob receive them (13:17). In 2 Maccabees the brothers hope for the resurrection of the body (2 Maccabees 7:9, "the King of the world will raise us, who died for his laws, to live again forever"); 4 Maccabees speaks instead of immortal souls. Jesus' story of the poor man "carried off by the angels to Abraham's embrace" (Luke 16:22) and his saying about the patriarchs, "for to him all are alive" (Luke 20:38), are the closest New Testament words. The difference from 2 Maccabees is discussed on the topic page for the soul.

p: 2 Maccabees says only that he went to the torture frame and died under blows. 4 Maccabees describes every stage.
b: 2 Maccabees 6:19 says, "Freely he walked toward the torture frame", and 6:30 that he died "under the blows". 4 Maccabees adds stripping, binding, whipping, kicking, fire and stinking liquids poured into his nose (6:2-25). The detail serves the thesis: the more the body suffers, the clearer it is that reason rules. The speech does not linger for shock: each stage ends with Eleazar unmoved (6:5, 7, 9-10).

a: as if he were being tortured in a dream
p: The old man's mind is so firm that the torture seems not to reach him.
b: The picture is that pain touches the body but not the self that reasons. 2 Maccabees puts it in Eleazar's own words: "In my body I bear cruel pains from the whip, but in my soul I suffer this with joy, because of my fear of him" (2 Maccabees 6:30). 4 Maccabees never denies the pain (6:7 says his body could not stand it) but shows that it did not move his reason.

a: Like a noble athlete taking blows
p: The martyr as an athlete in a contest who wins by holding out. A favorite picture of early Christian writers too.
b: Athlētēs is a competitor in the games, and the blows suggest boxing or the Greek all-in fighting. The speaker develops the picture fully at 17:11-16, where the martyrs' deaths are a contest with God as judge and immortality as the prize. Hebrews 12:1-2 sets Christians in the stadium before "so huge a cloud of witnesses" and tells them to run "with endurance"; Paul too speaks of training for a prize (1 Corinthians 9:24-27).

a: You just pretend to taste the pork
p: As in 2 Maccabees 6:21, old friends offer a way out: eat permitted meat and pretend it is pork.
b: 2 Maccabees has the men in charge of the sacrifice take Eleazar aside and urge him "to bring in meat he was permitted to use, prepared by himself, and to act as though he were eating" (2 Maccabees 6:21). 4 Maccabees gives the offer to "some of the king's men" who knew him (6:13), and has them set out "cooked food". The verb hypokrinomai, "pretend, play a part", is the root of English "hypocrite", and Eleazar takes it up at once: he will not "act out a play" (6:17).

p: Eleazar speaks to all faithful Jews as Abraham's children, a title the book uses often.
b: "Abraham's children" (Abraam paides) appears here and at 6:22, and the speaker calls the brothers "Abraham's children" too (9:21; 18:1, 23). Abraham was remembered as the one who was tested and held firm, ready to give up his son (Genesis 22), as this book recalls at 16:20. In the Gospels the title is debated: John the Baptist warns that God can raise up children for Abraham from stones (Matthew 3:9), and Jesus says Abraham's children would do Abraham's works (John 8:39). Paul makes all who believe Abraham's children (Galatians 3:7).

a: a model of ungodliness for the young
p: The heart of Eleazar's reason, in both books: his act would teach the young.
b: In 2 Maccabees he says, "Through my pretending ... they would be led astray because of me", and he dies to "leave behind a fine pattern" for the young (2 Maccabees 6:25, 28). 4 Maccabees uses typos, "pattern, model", and paradeigma, "example". Paul uses typos when he tells Timothy, "Be a model for the believers" (1 Timothy 4:12), and Peter when he tells elders to "be patterns for the flock" (1 Peter 5:3).

p: A detail not in 2 Maccabees: liquids poured into his nostrils to choke him.
b: The Greek chylos is a juice or liquid; "foul-smelling" (dysōdēs) suggests a brew made to suffocate or sicken. The instruments are "cruelly crafted" (kakotechnos, "made with evil skill"). The verb Swete prints, hyperiptosan, is rare and unclear. It looks like a form of hyperriptō, "throw over", which the lexicon of Liddell and Scott knows only of throwing the arm over a bar. The Plain English Translation supplies "the fire" from the context ("to burn him"), and Brenton's English has only "burnt him on the fire". Other meanings are possible.

a: You know, God, that I could have saved myself
p: His last words, like those in 2 Maccabees 6:30, begin with God's knowledge: he could have escaped.
b: 2 Maccabees has: "To the Lord, who holds holy knowledge, it is plain that I could have been let off from death" (2 Maccabees 6:30). Both books stress that the death is chosen: Eleazar could have saved himself. 4 Maccabees then adds what 2 Maccabees does not have, a prayer for the nation (6:28-29). The emphasis on free choice prepares for what follows: only a death freely given could be offered for others. Compare Jesus: "No one takes it away from me. I lay it down by my own choice" (John 10:18).

p: Hileōs genou: the Greek Bible's plea that God be gracious and forgive, from the same root as the atonement words.
b: Hileōs means gracious or merciful, and "be merciful" is the plea of Moses and the prophets for Israel (in the Greek of Exodus 32:12, "be merciful toward the evil of your people"). The same root gives hilaskomai, "make atonement", and hilastērion, the atonement lid of the ark (Hebrews 9:5) and the word the speaker uses at 17:22. The tax collector prays with the related verb: "God, be gracious to me, the sinner" (Luke 18:13). The deep section on the chapter page sets the whole prayer in its background.

a: Let the penalty we pay on their account be enough for you
p: Eleazar asks God to count his own suffering as enough for the nation's punishment.
b: Dikē here is penalty or punishment, and arkestheis, "being satisfied", asks God to accept it as sufficient. The prayer assumes the reading of 2 Maccabees: the persecution is God's discipline for the nation's sin (2 Maccabees 6:12-16; 7:18, 32-33). Eleazar offers his suffering so that the discipline may end. Codex Sinaiticus reads hyper autōn, "on their behalf", for peri autōn, "on their account" (see the variant); hyper is the word of Paul's "Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8).
orig: ἀρκεσθεὶς τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ περὶ αὐτῶν δίκῃ (arkestheis tē hēmetera peri autōn dikē)

t: Compared with the Bible: a martyr's blood as cleansing and exchange
p: Eleazar asks that his blood cleanse the nation and that God take his soul as a life in exchange for the people.
b: What it says. Katharsion is a means of purifying, used in Greek for cleansing sacrifices; antipsychon, "a life in exchange", is used in this book only here and at 17:22. Eleazar asks God to treat his blood like a cleansing offering and to take his soul as a substitute for the people. Background: "It is the blood that makes atonement, by means of the life in it" (Leviticus 17:11); the servant who "was pierced because of our rebellions" (Isaiah 53:5); and the youngest brother's prayer that God stop his anger "in me and my brothers" (2 Maccabees 7:38). Agrees with the Bible's pattern of a righteous one suffering for others (Isaiah 53:10-12; Exodus 32:32). Goes beyond the Old Testament in giving the role to a martyr's death; the New Testament gives it to Jesus' death (Mark 10:45; Hebrews 9:12-14). Whether a believer's suffering can share in it (compare Colossians 1:24) is asked on the 2 Maccabees 7 card. See the chapter page.
r: Leviticus 17:11; Isaiah 53:5; Isaiah 53:10-12; 2 Maccabees 7:37-38; 17:20-22; Mark 10:45; Romans 3:25; Hebrews 9:12-14; 1 John 1:7; Colossians 1:24

a: take my soul as a life in exchange for them
p: Antipsychon: anti, "in place of", and psychē, "life, soul". Mark 10:45's "ransom in place of many" uses the same anti.
b: The word means something given "in place of a life". The Greek psychē is both "life" and "soul": the Plain English Translation says "soul", as for psychē elsewhere in the book, and keeps "a life in exchange" for antipsychon, so that both senses are heard. Jesus says that the Son of Man came "to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (Mark 10:45), where "life" is psychē and "in place of" is anti. The likeness of language is clear; whether the Gospel writer or Paul knew 4 Maccabees is unproven. Proposed dates for 4 Maccabees run from about AD 20 to the early second century (see the note on 4:2), so it may be earlier or later than Mark. The same term returns at 17:22, where the martyrs become "a life in exchange for the nation's sin".

p: Hieros, "holy", the word for temple things. The priest dies like a sacrifice.
b: The adjective hieros is used of sacred things: the temple (hieron), priests, offerings. Calling Eleazar "the holy man" just after his prayer fits the book's picture of his death as an offering. He dies "noble" (eugenōs, "as a well-born man") and held firm "by reason", so the story returns to the thesis at once (6:31).

a: Beyond all doubt, then, godly reason is master over the passions
p: After Eleazar's death the speaker states his thesis as proven. Chapters 7-18 add the brothers and the mother.
b: Homologoumenōs, "admittedly, by common agreement", is a debater's word: the point is now granted. The conclusion (6:31-35) repeats the thesis of 1:1 in the same words, with despotēs, "master", and adds that reason rules not only pains but pleasures (6:35), so the argument circles back to its start. Chapter 7 then praises Eleazar at length.
